t.la pena de candamo@43.5,-6.1:
In the hills above the Nalón valley in Asturias, a cave hides one of the great collections of Paleolithic art in Spain. The Cueva de la Peña de Candamo, near San Román de Candamo, was discovered in 1914 and contains paintings and engravings of horses, bison, deer, goats and other animals, made during the Upper Paleolithic, and a remarkable wall of engraved figures. It is part of the UNESCO listing of cave art in northern Spain, and unlike some other caves, it can be visited, though only in limited numbers and for part of the year, so book ahead.

The Nalón valley, in central Asturias, is green and fertile, with meadows, apple orchards and forests of chestnut and oak, and the river winds toward the sea at San Esteban de Pravia. The area is known for its kiwi farms, and for the cider of Asturias, which is poured from a height to aerate it, a skill that locals perform with style. Grado, about eight kilometres away, is an old market town, and its market days bring in local produce, cheeses and crafts from the surrounding villages.

Asturias is a paradise for motorcyclists. The roads are endlessly twisty, climbing through green valleys and over mountain passes, with spectacular views of the Picos de Europa and the Cantabrian mountains. From Grado, roads lead west toward the coast at Cudillero, a fishing village of colourful houses built into a ravine, and south into the mountains, toward the Somiedo natural park, home to brown bears. Traffic is light, but roads can be narrow and wet, and cows on the road are a regular hazard. The weather is mild but changeable, and rain is frequent, so be prepared.

Grado has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Oviedo, the capital of Asturias, is about twenty-five kilometres away, with its cathedral and pre-Romanesque churches, Santa María del Naranco and San Miguel de Lillo, on a hill above the city. Asturian food is hearty: fabada, a stew of white beans with chorizo and black pudding, cachopo, a huge breaded veal steak stuffed with ham and cheese, and cheeses like Cabrales, a strong blue cheese matured in mountain caves.
t.chemin de l interieur@43.3,-7.8:
Pilgrims have been crossing this green upland of Galicia on their way to Santiago de Compostela for more than a thousand years, and the scallop-shell waymarkers still guide them through the villages around Vilalba and Guitiriz. This is the Terra Chá, the flat land, a high plateau in the north of the province of Lugo where the northern pilgrim routes come down from the Cantabrian coast toward the interior. The Ways of Saint James in northern Spain are part of a UNESCO listing that recognises not only the famous French Way but also the coastal and inland routes that run through this region.

The landscape is gentle and rural: fields divided by stone walls, small oak and chestnut woods, scattered farms with their raised granaries, the hórreos, and streams winding through wet meadows. The Miño river rises not far from here, at the beginning of its long journey south toward Portugal. Rain and mist are frequent visitors, and the green is the kind that only comes with plenty of water.

The riding is relaxed rather than dramatic. Roads on the plateau are mostly smooth, with gentle curves and light traffic, crossing open farmland and passing through quiet villages. Toward the north and east the land rises into hills with tighter, more interesting roads, and the coast of A Mariña is within reach for a day ride. Beware of wet leaves, cattle being moved between fields and pilgrims walking along the roadside, especially in summer when the routes are busiest.

Vilalba is the main town nearby, with fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants. Its castle tower, once the stronghold of the Andrade family, now houses a parador. The town is also known for San Simón da Costa, a smoked pear-shaped cheese produced in the surrounding area, and for its rich local cooking. Guitiriz, the other neighbour, has a long tradition as a spa town with mineral waters.

Galician food is a reason in itself to come: octopus with paprika and olive oil, hearty caldo gallego soup, local beef and crusty bread from wood-fired ovens. May, June and September tend to give the kindest weather and the thinnest stream of pilgrims. Even in rain, a ride across the Terra Chá has a peaceful, timeless quality, the road threading through a land where people have walked toward the same city for centuries.
t.faia vale afonsinho@40.9,-7.1:
Thirty thousand years ago, give or take, people in this valley scratched horses, aurochs and ibex into the schist rocks along the River Côa, and their drawings would almost certainly have been drowned if a dam had been built here in the 1990s. Instead, after a fierce campaign, the dam was abandoned and the Côa Valley rock art became one of the most important open-air Palaeolithic art sites in the world, listed by UNESCO in 1998 together with Siega Verde across the border in Spain. Faia, in the side valley near Vale Afonsinho, is one of its core sites, with engravings and some rare painted figures on the rock faces above the river.

Visits to the rock art sites are by guided tour only, arranged through the Côa Museum in Vila Nova de Foz Côa, a striking modern building set into the hillside above the valley. The tours, often in four-wheel-drive vehicles over rough tracks, take you to the rocks at the best times of day for seeing the engravings, when low light brings out the lines.

The landscape is rugged and beautiful: steep valleys, terraced slopes planted with almonds, olives and vines, and the Douro winding through deep gorges to the north. The Douro wine region, also UNESCO-listed, begins here, and its terraced vineyards are one of the great sights of Portugal. In February the almond trees around Foz Côa burst into white and pink blossom, a celebrated spectacle.

The riding is superb. Roads wind through the valleys and over the hills, with tight curves, steep gradients and spectacular views. The N222 along the Douro, between Peso da Régua and Pinhão, is often called one of the best driving roads in the world, and the roads around Foz Côa and Meda are quieter but just as twisty. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, farm vehicles and the occasional wandering dog.

Vila Nova de Foz Côa, about seventeen kilometres away, has fuel, food and accommodation. Local food includes roast kid, cured meats, cheese and, of course, port and Douro wines. Come in late winter for the almond blossom, or in autumn for the grape harvest. Summers are very hot. Stand before an engraved horse on a rock above the river, its lines faint but sure, and feel the extraordinary span of human time.
t.eglise et monastere de san salvador@43.4:
Pilgrims have been trudging past these walls for about a thousand years, which makes a motorcycle look like a rather recent idea. The monastery of San Salvador de Cornellana stands beside the Narcea river in central Asturias, on the old inland route to Santiago that runs west from Oviedo through Grado and Salas. It was founded in the eleventh century, passed to the Benedictines of Cluny, and the church that survives keeps Romanesque bones under later remodelling. The bulk of the cloister and the old monastic buildings give the little village a weight that seems out of proportion to its size.

This is the Camino Primitivo, the oldest of the pilgrim ways, said to follow the path taken by King Alfonso II of Asturias to the newly found tomb of St James in the ninth century. You will see the walkers, scallop shells swinging from their packs, and they will see you, so ride through the village gently. Asturias treats them well: there are hostels and cafés in every town and the locals are used to strangers asking for directions in four languages.

The Narcea is a famous salmon river, and the valley around Cornellana is the green, damp Spain that surprises people expecting sunshine. Chestnut and oak cover the slopes, cows graze between stone barns on stilts called hórreos, and cloud often sits low on the hills in the morning. The roads are a joy if you like your corners linked and endless: the old road west toward Salas climbs through wooded hills with smooth curves and modest traffic, since most through traffic now uses the motorway. Rain is a fact of life here at any season, and wet leaves in autumn deserve respect.

Grado, seven kilometres away, has fuel, a weekly market and plenty of places to eat; Salas, a little further west, has a medieval tower and the tomb of Fernando de Valdés, the sixteenth-century Inquisitor General who was born there. Asturian food deserves the stop: fabada with its creamy white beans and smoked meats, local cheeses, and cider poured from a great height by a waiter who has practised it for years. The cider is low in alcohol, but still not for riders. A café con leche and a slice of something sweet will do just as well before you carry on west.
t.prehistoric rock art sites in the coa va:
On the Spanish side of the border with Portugal, the river Águeda cuts through granite and schist on its way to the Douro, and on the rock faces along its banks, at Siega Verde, Palaeolithic people engraved horses, aurochs, deer and goats more than ten thousand years ago. In 2010 Siega Verde was added to the Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley, the Portuguese World Heritage Site just across the border, recognising that these open-air engravings form one of the largest collections of Ice Age art in the world.

What makes these sites special is that the art is outdoors, not hidden in caves. The engravings are pecked or scratched into vertical rock surfaces near the river, sometimes overlapping, sometimes showing animals with multiple heads to suggest movement. They are best seen in low-angled light, early morning or late afternoon, when the shadows bring out the lines. Guided visits are the way to see them properly.

The landscape is the dehesa of western Salamanca: rolling plains with holm oaks and cork oaks, stone walls, cattle and black Iberian pigs foraging for acorns. It is a quiet, spacious country, hot and dry in summer, cold in winter, with spring bringing green grass and wildflowers. Villages such as Castillejo de Martín Viejo and Villar de Ciervo are small and peaceful.

The nearest town of size is Ciudad Rodrigo, fifteen kilometres away, a walled hilltop town with a cathedral, a castle converted into a parador and a long military history. In January 1812, during the Peninsular War, Wellington's army stormed the town after a short siege, and marks of the fighting can still be seen. The town is a good base, with fuel, hotels, restaurants and shops.

Nobody comes here for knee-down riding. Roads through the dehesa are straight or gently curving, with little traffic and good surfaces. To the north, the Arribes del Duero offer dramatic canyon roads along the Portuguese border, and to the south the Sierra de Gata and Sierra de Francia provide mountain curves and villages of stone and timber. Food is excellent: Iberian ham, farinato sausage from Ciudad Rodrigo and roast lamb or suckling pig, with wines from the Arribes or the nearby Douro.
t.historic centre of oporto@41.1,-8.6:
Porto is a city built on a granite slope above the Douro, and for a rider that means two things immediately: the views are wonderful, and the streets are steep, narrow and paved with stone that turns slippery as soap in the rain. Tram rails cross the old centre, cobbles are everywhere, and traffic is dense, so the best plan is to park the bike once and walk. The historic centre, from the riverside quarter of Ribeira up to the cathedral and the Clérigos Tower, was listed by UNESCO in 1996.

Ribeira is the heart of the old port: tall, narrow houses in faded colours piled up above the quay, washing hanging from balconies, and cafés along the river where the old rabelo boats, which once carried barrels of wine down from the vineyards, are moored. Above it, the double-decker iron arch of the Dom Luís I bridge spans the gorge, designed by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Gustave Eiffel, and opened in the 1880s. Walk across the upper deck, now used by the metro, for the classic view of the city.

On the far bank, in Vila Nova de Gaia, are the lodges where port wine is aged and blended. Port takes its name from the city, but the grapes are grown upriver in the Douro valley, the oldest demarcated wine region in the world, and the wine was traditionally brought down to Gaia to mature. Many lodges offer tours and tastings. Back on the Porto side, the São Bento railway station is worth a stop for its entrance hall lined with blue and white azulejo tiles depicting scenes from Portuguese history.

The great ride from here is up the Douro valley itself. The N222 between Peso da Régua and Pinhão is often called one of the best roads in the world: a ribbon of tarmac along the river, under steep terraced vineyards, with endless curves and views. It is about two hours from Porto, and makes a perfect day out, ideally on a weekday in spring or during the harvest in September and early October.

Fuel and everything else are easy in Porto. The city's signature dish is the francesinha, a sandwich of ham, sausage and steak covered in melted cheese and a spicy beer and tomato sauce, which is not light but is unforgettable. Then sit on the river wall in the evening with a glass of white port and tonic and watch the light fade on the bridge.
t.chemin primitif@43.3,-6.4:
Tineo stands on a hillside above the green valleys of western Asturias, and it is one of the main stops on the Camino Primitivo, the original Way of St James. According to tradition, it was King Alfonso II of Asturias who first walked from Oviedo to Santiago in the ninth century to see the tomb, newly found, of the apostle, and the route he took became the Primitivo. It is the hardest of the Caminos, crossing mountain after mountain, and the pilgrims you meet here, wet, muddy and cheerful, are a special breed.

Tineo itself is a market town of about ten thousand, with stone houses, a Franciscan church and a promenade with a view over the hills. Its cattle markets have long been important in a region where cows outnumber people, and the surrounding hills were home to the vaqueiros de alzada, herdsmen who moved with their cattle between summer and winter pastures and had their own distinct traditions. The town is also known for its cured sausage and for the local version of fabada, the white bean stew of Asturias.

West of Tineo, the pilgrim route divides. The harder option, the Hospitales route, climbs over the high, bare mountains towards Pola de Allande, while the road follows the valleys. On a bike, the AS-14 from Pola de Allande over the Puerto del Palo is the one to do: it climbs in long switchbacks to over a thousand metres, with views across wild, heather-covered ridges and almost no traffic. Descending towards Grandas de Salime, you reach the huge reservoir of the Navia, a vast sheet of water hemmed in by steep slopes.

The roads in this part of Asturias are twisty, narrow and often wet. The Atlantic delivers rain in every season, and fog clings to the passes, so expect slippery surfaces and limited visibility. On a clear day, though, the colours are intense, every shade of green against grey stone and blue sky. Summer is the safest season; winter can bring snow to the passes.

Tineo has fuel and several places to eat, and Salas, to the east, is another option. Stop for a cider, poured from a height to aerate it, and drink it quickly before it goes flat, as Asturians do.
t.sanctuary of bom jesus do monte in braga:
There are 577 steps up to Bom Jesus do Monte, and a good many pilgrims still climb them on their knees. The sanctuary hangs on a wooded hillside above Braga, in the green Minho of northern Portugal, and what makes it extraordinary is the staircase. It zigzags up the slope in a series of baroque landings, each with its own fountain, chapel or statues, and each telling a different part of the story, from the five senses to the three virtues. Work began in the early eighteenth century and went on for decades, and the white church at the top, with its twin towers, was finished later, in neoclassical style. UNESCO listed the whole ensemble in 2019.

You can cheat. A funicular, built in 1882 and driven by water ballast, still runs up beside the stairs, and it is said to be the oldest of its kind on the Iberian Peninsula. Two cabins balance each other, and water pumped into the upper one makes it heavier so it pulls the lower one up. The ride is slow and utterly charming, and it is a good way to see the staircase from the side.

Braga itself is one of the oldest Christian cities in Portugal, with a cathedral that was begun in the eleventh century and a long reputation as the country's religious capital, and Holy Week brings processions that fill the streets. With around a hundred and twenty thousand people it has fuel, parking and plenty of restaurants, though the narrow centre is better walked. The nearby village of Adaúfe is a quiet spot to eat lunch.

For a rider, Braga is the gateway to the hills. East of the city the roads climb through chestnut and oak woods, small farms and granite villages with stone granaries on stilts, and then up to the Peneda-Gerês National Park, where bends tighten and wild Garrano ponies stand in the road. Surfaces are generally good, but they can be wet and slippery with leaf litter, and mist is common in the morning. The best months are May, June and September, when the hillsides are green and the roads are not packed. Take a glass of vinho verde with grilled sardines or a plate of bacalhau, and stay for the sunset from the top of the stairs.
t.camara santa de oviedo@43.4,-5.8:
Oviedo is a surprise, a small, green, rainy capital with an almost Alpine smell of woodsmoke and a history that begins with a king. In the early ninth century Alfonso II, called the Chaste, moved his court here and began building churches in a style now called Asturian pre-Romanesque, which is unlike anything else in Spain, with tall narrow proportions, round arches and decorated stone. The Cámara Santa is a chapel inside the cathedral of San Salvador, built to protect relics and treasures, and it still holds the Cross of the Angels, dated to 808, and the Cross of Victory, which belonged to the later king Alfonso III and became the emblem of Asturias. UNESCO included the city's early monuments in its list in 1985.

On the hill of Naranco above the city stand two more buildings from the same era: Santa María del Naranco, a royal hall that later became a church, and San Miguel de Lillo, a smaller chapel with strange, flat carvings. Santa Cristina de Lena, in the hills to the south, is another of them. All are well worth the ride, and the roads up to Naranco are pleasant and easy, with tight bends through oak and chestnut, and views over the city.

Riding in Asturias means rain, so be prepared. The weather comes off the Bay of Biscay and drops on the Cantabrian mountains, and the result is a lush, green country where the roads are often wet and the verges thick with ferns and brambles. When the sun comes out, it is glorious, and the mountains of the Picos de Europa and the high passes of the Cordillera, such as the Pajares, give some of the best riding in northern Spain. Oviedo itself has more than two hundred thousand people, with every service imaginable, and the old town is largely pedestrian. Leave the bike in a garage.

The Camino Primitivo, the oldest pilgrim route to Santiago, starts in Oviedo, and you will see walkers with scallop shells in the streets. Cider is the local drink, poured from a height in a thin stream to aerate it, and the city has a whole street of cider houses, the Calle Gascona. Order a fabada, the bean stew with chorizo and morcilla, and do not plan anything demanding for the afternoon.
t.routes of santiago de compostela camino:
Tineo sits on a ridge in western Asturias, and for pilgrims walking the Camino Primitivo it is the place where the real mountains begin. This is the oldest of the routes to Santiago, said to have been walked by King Alfonso II in the ninth century when he went from Oviedo to the tomb of St James, and it climbs from the green hills around Oviedo into a wilder landscape of ridges and valleys that separates Asturias from Galicia. The town itself has about 11,000 people, a handsome old centre, a church and a pilgrim hostel, and the Camino passes through it on the way west.

The route from here has a famous variant, the Hospitales, a high-level path along a ridge that follows an old trail past the ruins of medieval pilgrim hospices, with long views across the mountains. It is a walkers' route, not a road, though roads that cross the same hills give riders much of the same scenery. Landscape here is a patchwork of meadow, chestnut, oak and gorse, with villages of grey stone and slate roofs, and the weather is often misty and damp, as the Atlantic air pushes against the mountains.

The riding in western Asturias is rewarding. Roads wind along ridges and down into deep valleys, with plenty of bends, some of them tight, and surfaces that vary from smooth to patched. Cattle and tractors on the road are normal, and mist can make visibility poor, especially in the morning. Spring and early autumn are the best times, with green hills and clear air, though rain is possible at any time. Check the weather before heading up to higher roads.

Tineo has fuel stations, shops and several places to eat, and it is a sensible overnight stop. Asturian food is generous, with fabada, a stew of white beans with sausage and pork, and a strong tradition of cheese, including Cabrales and others made in the mountains. The local drink is sidra, a dry cider, which is poured from a height into a wide glass, a ritual known as escanciar. If you see walkers with scallop shells on their rucksacks, give them room and a wave, since a rider's pace and a pilgrim's are very different.
t.chuh nuur lake cluster@49.5,114.6:
Open steppe, a few shallow lakes and a very large sky: that is the landscape of Dauria, the borderland where eastern Mongolia meets Russia and China. The Chuh-Nuur lakes lie in the Mongolian part of it, a region of rolling grassland dotted with salt-edged basins that fill and shrink with the rains. UNESCO lists the Landscapes of Dauria as a transboundary site, because it is the migration crossroads that matters, not the border drawn across it.

The reason to care is birds. Dauria is on a flyway used by cranes, geese, swans and waders, and several crane species stop here, among them white-naped and red-crowned cranes, while Siberian cranes pass through in much smaller numbers. Mongolian gazelles travel the steppe in big herds, sometimes in the thousands, and can cross a road in front of you at astonishing speed. The grass is short and wind-combed, and in a dry year the lakes can almost vanish. In a wet year the shores are alive with sound.

Riding here means tracks more than roads. There is no town near the coordinates, so you are in remote country, and you should plan as you would for any steppe crossing: spare fuel, water, a satellite messenger if you have one, and a clear idea of where the next settlement is. Surfaces are a mix of packed earth, sand and washboard, and after rain the dirt can become sticky. Navigation is by GPS, because tracks braid and split and herders' paths can look more convincing than they are.

Weather is the second challenge. Summers are warm and can bring sudden storms, while winters are bitterly cold and the wind off the steppe never really stops. Late spring and early autumn are the best times for birds, and early mornings are best for light. The herders you meet are generous with tea and curiosity, and will usually know the state of the tracks better than any map. Be polite about gates and animals, leave nothing behind, and let the quiet work on you for a while before you start the engine again.
t.cathedrale san salvador et chambre saint:
Oviedo wears its history lightly, and it is a surprisingly relaxed city, a green, rain-washed place of nearly a quarter of a million people at the foot of the Cantabrian mountains. Its Gothic cathedral, San Salvador, rises over the old town, but the real treasure is hidden inside: the Cámara Santa, the Holy Chamber, a small pre-Romanesque chapel built in the ninth century when King Alfonso II the Chaste made Oviedo the capital of the little Christian kingdom of Asturias. It holds the great relics of the Asturian monarchy, including two gold-and-jewel crosses, the Cross of the Angels and the Cross of Victory, which has become the symbol of the region, and a chest of relics that pilgrims came from across Europe to see.

That pilgrim tradition is worth remembering. The Camino Primitivo, the original route to Santiago de Compostela, begins here, following the path of Alfonso II himself when he went to see the newly found tomb of the apostle. Medieval proverbs said that whoever goes to Santiago and not to Oviedo visits the servant and neglects the Lord, a bit of local promotion that still raises a smile.

Asturias is also cider country, and Oviedo has a whole street, the Calle Gascona, lined with sidrerías where the cider is poured from a great height into the glass, to aerate it, a skill that takes years to master. Try the cider, a plate of fabada, the local bean stew, and a slice of cheese, and you will understand what the city does best. Pre-Romanesque churches stand on the hills above the town, including Santa María del Naranco, and they are well worth a detour.

Riding in the city is not hard, though the rain can make the cobbles slick and the old town streets awkward. Parking a motorbike is easy at the edge of the pedestrian centre. Fuel is no problem in a city of this size, and Lugones, to the north-west, has plenty of stations and shops. The mountains to the south, with their long, flowing roads, make a wonderful playground if the weather behaves.
t.cathedral de lugo@43.0,-7.6:
Lugo is one of those cities that tells you its age before you have parked. A ring of Roman wall, two kilometres of it and still complete, circles the old town, and walking along the top is the best way to understand why UNESCO listed it. The Romans founded Lucus Augusti here at the end of the first century before Christ, drawn by hot springs on the Miño river, and the baths are still in use by the riverside. The wall's gates, rebuilt and re-cut many times, let you walk in and out of the old quarter as people have for nearly two thousand years.

The cathedral sits in the middle of the old town and is a mixture of centuries. It began as a Romanesque church, took on Gothic parts, then a baroque front, and in the end has a character that comes from all of it. It is known for keeping the Blessed Sacrament permanently on display, which is a rarity. The Plaza de Santa María in front is a good place for a coffee.

Riding in is easy from almost any direction. The roads from Sobrado dos Monxes and Mondoñedo come across rolling Galician countryside: green, damp, lined with granite walls and eucalyptus, with plenty of bends and occasional slippery patches in the wet. This is rain country, and a waterproof layer is not optional. The city has well over ninety thousand people, so fuel, repair shops and hotels are no problem, and parking a motorbike near the wall is usually easy outside market days.

Lugo is also a city to eat in. Tapas arrive with drinks in many bars, which makes an evening stroll cheap and unhurried. Octopus cooked Galician style at the fairs, pork and chestnuts in the autumn, and the local cheeses all reward a long lunch. The Camino Primitivo, the oldest pilgrim route to Santiago, passes through the city, so you will meet walkers with sunburnt knees in the lanes around the wall. Spring and September are the best months, when the stone is warm and the sky is not yet solid grey.
t.zone archeologique d art rupestre de sie:
Eighteen thousand years is a conservative guess for some of the engravings on the rocks at Siega Verde, and the animals they show are still recognisable: horses, aurochs, deer, ibex and the occasional bison, scratched with flint into the flat grey-brown schist slabs that line the river Agueda. There are hundreds of them, and the open-air gallery runs for about a kilometre along the water. They were made by hunter-gatherers of the Upper Palaeolithic, and they are all outdoors, unprotected by caves, which makes the survival of so much of it remarkable. The site was found only in 1988 by a pair of archaeologists, and it was added to the World Heritage list in 2010 as an extension of the Coa Valley in Portugal, which has a related collection less than a hundred kilometres away.

Visits are by guided walk, and it is worth booking ahead. A guide shows you where to look, and angled light can bring out lines you would walk past. In the early morning or late afternoon, with the sun slanting across the stone, a horse's head or a pair of antlers suddenly appears out of the rock.

The setting is dehesa, the open woodland of holm oak and cork oak that covers much of western Spain, where black Iberian pigs feed on acorns and become the finest ham in the world. The nearest town is Ciudad Rodrigo, about fifteen kilometres away, a small fortified city on a hill above the river with a medieval cathedral, a castle that now houses a parador and a complete circuit of walls that was fought over in the Peninsular War. It has fuel, food and plenty of bars serving tapas. The village of Castillejo de Martin Viejo is closer but tiny.

Riding in this part of Castilla y Leon is relaxed. Roads are quiet and well surfaced, with long straights across the plateau, and the wooded ranges of the Sierra de Francia to the south offer twistier riding and villages of timbered houses, such as La Alberca. Summers are hot and winters are cold and wet, so spring and autumn are best.

Try the local hornazo, a pastry filled with ham and chorizo, and a glass of Rueda or Toro wine.
t.salamanca@41.0,-5.7:
Salamanca glows. Its buildings are built from a golden sandstone that takes on a honey colour in low sun, and the effect, especially in the late afternoon in the Plaza Mayor, is memorable. The city stands on the Tormes river in western Spain, about 800 metres above sea level, and is one of the great university towns of Europe, with a student population that gives the old streets life well into the night.

The university, founded in 1218, is among the oldest in the world, and its carved facade is a famous challenge: a tiny frog hides in the stonework, and tradition says that students who find it without help will pass their exams. The Casa de las Conchas, covered in carved scallop shells, is another landmark. The city has two cathedrals, old and new, which stand side by side, and the Plaza Mayor is among the finest baroque squares in Spain, a place where residents come to stroll and meet.

The ride north follows the Ruta de la Plata, the Silver Route, an old Roman road that once linked Mérida in the south with Astorga in the north. The name has nothing to do with silver; it probably derives from an Arabic word meaning paved road. Today you can follow it on modern highways, with long, easy stretches through dehesa, open oak pasture where black Iberian pigs forage, and wheat fields stretching to the horizon. Summer is hot and dry, spring is green and pleasant, and winter can be cold and foggy. Traffic is light outside the city.

Salamanca has fuel stations around its ring roads, an abundance of tapas bars, and places to stay at all prices. Santa Marta de Tormes, close by, also has plenty of services. Parking in the old centre is restricted, so use a garage or leave the bike at your hotel. Try jamón ibérico and the regional hornazo pastry, and give yourself time for an evening paseo under the lights.
Coimbra's university is one of the oldest in Europe, founded in 1290 in Lisbon and finally settled in Coimbra in 1537, when King João III installed it in the old royal palace on the hill. The Alta, the upper town, grew around it, and the whole hill, along with Rua da Sofia below, is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Students still walk the lanes in black capes, and the city is built around them in a way few other towns in Europe still are.

The jewel of the complex is the Joanina Library, a Baroque hall of the early eighteenth century with gilded bookcases, painted ceilings and some sixty thousand old volumes. The roads are narrow and winding, with many junctions, and are generally quiet, though you will share them with tractors, cows and walkers. Watch out for wet leaves and mud in autumn and winter.

Sobrado is a small village with a few bars and shops, but for a reliable fuel stop, head to Arzúa, sixteen kilometres away, a town on the Camino Francés famous for its creamy cow's milk cheese. Galician food is excellent: pulpo á feira, octopus with paprika and olive oil, caldo galego, empanada and the local wines. Santiago de Compostela is about an hour's ride to the west, and Lugo, with its intact Roman walls, about the same distance to the east.
t.eglise santa maria de soto de luina@43.6:
Soto de Luiña is a quiet parish in western Asturias, a short way inland from one of the wildest stretches of the Cantabrian coast, and its church of Santa María is the reason the village has a name beyond the region. The building is baroque, rebuilt in the eighteenth century around older foundations, and alongside it stands the former pilgrims' hospital that once took in walkers on the coastal Way of Saint James. The church's interior, with its gilded altarpieces, comes as a surprise in such a small place, and the whole ensemble gives a sense of how the Camino shaped even modest villages along the route.

Cudillero, the nearest town of any size, lies about seven kilometres east, and is famous for the way its brightly painted houses crowd up the sides of a narrow valley above the fishing harbour, like an audience in a steep amphitheatre. It is busy in summer and worth seeing anyway, especially for grilled fish and a glass of Asturian cider poured from a height. Fuel and supplies are easy to find there and in the larger towns along the coast towards Avilés.

The riding here is all about the coast and the green hills behind it. A modern motorway now carries through traffic, which leaves the old coastal road for the curious, and that old road is the better choice by far, rising and falling through eucalyptus and chestnut, dipping to river mouths and climbing again over headlands. Nearby beaches such as the Playa del Silencio, a curve of grey pebbles under high cliffs, are reached by short side roads and a walk. The surfaces are generally sound but can be slippery when wet, and wet is the normal state of affairs here for a good part of the year.

That rain is the price of the landscape. Western Asturias is green because the Atlantic weather arrives straight off the sea, and fog can roll in over the headlands within minutes on a summer afternoon, turning a bright ride into a damp, grey one. The reward is the smell of cut grass, salt and wood smoke, the sound of the sea against slate cliffs, and evenings that end with a plate of fabada or fresh seafood. Pack a waterproof layer whatever the forecast promises.
t.historic centre of guimaraes and couros:
Aqui nasceu Portugal, says the slogan painted on an old section of the town wall: Portugal was born here. Guimarães claims to be the cradle of the nation because Afonso Henriques, the first king of Portugal, is said to have been born here, and in 1128 he won the battle of São Mamede nearby, against his mother's forces, a key step towards independence. The castle on the hill, a compact fortress with a tall keep, and the small Romanesque church beside it, where he is said to have been baptised, are the symbols of that story.

Below the castle, the Palace of the Dukes of Braganza, a vast fifteenth century building with forests of brick chimneys, looks more like something from northern France than Portugal. The historic centre, with its granite houses, wooden balconies and medieval squares, was listed by UNESCO in 2001, and in 2023 the listing was extended to include the Couros zone, the old tanning quarter along a stream just outside the walls, where leather was produced for centuries in stone tanks. Walking through the quarter, with its old tanneries, factory buildings and workers' houses, gives a sense of the industrial side of the town's history.

The riding around Guimarães is in the green, hilly country of the Minho, the north west corner of Portugal. The roads are often busy, especially near the towns, and the area is densely populated, with houses, factories and farms scattered along the roads. But there are good rides to be had, especially on the minor roads through the hills. The road up to Penha, a granite mountain above the town with a sanctuary, has tight bends and fine views, and there is also a cable car for those who prefer to leave the bike in town.

Guimarães, a city of about forty thousand people in its centre and many more around it, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. The local food is hearty: roasted meats, bacalhau, rojões, and the light, slightly sparkling vinho verde, the wine of the Minho. Braga, with the famous baroque staircase of Bom Jesus do Monte, is a short ride away, and Porto is less than an hour to the south. The climate is mild, but rain is common, especially in winter.
t.roman walls of lugo@43.0,-7.6:
Lugo is the only city in the world still completely surrounded by intact Roman walls. Built in the late third century, when the Roman Empire was under pressure from invasions, the walls run for more than two kilometres around the old town, with dozens of semicircular towers and ten gates, some Roman and some added later. They are wide enough at the top for a walkway, and walking the full circuit, with views over the rooftops of the old town on one side and the modern city on the other, is the best way to get a sense of the place. The walls were listed by UNESCO in 2000.

Inside the walls, the old town of Lugo is a pleasant maze of narrow streets, squares and old houses, with a cathedral that combines Romanesque, Gothic, baroque and neoclassical styles, and plenty of bars serving tapas and wine. Lugo is famous for its generous tapas culture, with a free plate of food often served with each drink. The city is also a stop on the Camino Primitivo, the oldest route of the Way of Saint James, which runs from Oviedo to Santiago de Compostela, and pilgrims with backpacks are a common sight in the streets.

The riding around Lugo is through the green, rolling countryside of inland Galicia, with fields, woods, small villages and stone farmhouses. The roads are generally good, with gentle bends and little traffic outside the main routes. To the south east, the mountains of the Ribeira Sacra offer spectacular riding, with roads winding along the steep slopes of the Miño and Sil canyons, past terraced vineyards and ancient monasteries. Further east, the Roman gold mines of Las Médulas, in the neighbouring region of El Bierzo, created a surreal landscape of red rock pinnacles and caves, and they are another UNESCO site worth the ride.

Lugo, a city of nearly a hundred thousand people, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. The local food is classic Galician: pulpo a feira, octopus boiled and served with paprika and olive oil, empanadas, beef from the local Rubia Gallega cattle, and the cheeses of the region, including the soft, mild tetilla. The weather is mild and wet, with rain likely at any time of year, and fog can settle in the valleys in autumn and winter.
t.tito bustillo@43.5,-5.1:
In 1968, a group of young cavers from Ribadesella found their way into a cave system beneath the Ardines hill, just outside the town, and stumbled upon an extraordinary gallery of Palaeolithic art: horses, deer and reindeer, painted in red and black, along with strange red symbols that some interpret as female figures. One of the group, Celestino Fernández Bustillo, known as Tito, died in a mountain accident a few days later, and the cave was named in his honour. Tito Bustillo is one of the most important painted caves in Europe, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of Cave of Altamira and Palaeolithic Cave Art of Northern Spain. Visits are limited in number and season to protect the art, and booking in advance is essential.

Next to the cave, a modern interpretation centre explains the art and the life of the people who made it, with reproductions and exhibitions, and it is well worth a visit, even if you cannot get into the cave itself. Ribadesella is a pleasant town at the mouth of the river Sella, with a harbour, a long sandy beach and a lively old quarter. Every year, on the first Saturday of August, the town hosts the International Descent of the Sella, a canoe race from Arriondas, about fifteen kilometres upstream, to Ribadesella, with thousands of participants and spectators and a massive party afterwards.

The riding in eastern Asturias is superb. The coast is rugged and beautiful, with cliffs, beaches and small fishing villages, and the roads along it wind over headlands and dip into coves. To the south, the Picos de Europa rise steeply from the coast, and the roads into the mountains, to Cangas de Onís, Covadonga and the lakes of Enol and Ercina, are spectacular, with tight bends, steep climbs and views over the peaks. The coast between Ribadesella and Colunga is known as the Dinosaur Coast, with fossil footprints in the rocks and a museum of the Jurassic at Colunga.

Ribadesella, a town of about six thousand people, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. The local food is classic Asturian: fabada, cachopo, seafood and cheeses, washed down with cider poured from a height. The weather is mild and wet, with rain likely at any time of year, and fog can roll in from the sea quickly.
t.santa cristina de lena@43.1,-5.8:
On a grassy knoll above the Lena valley, south of Oviedo, stands a tiny stone church that has watched over the main road between Asturias and Castile for more than a thousand years. Santa Cristina de Lena is one of the jewels of Asturian pre-Romanesque architecture, built in the ninth century when the little Christian kingdom of Asturias was the only part of Iberia outside Muslim rule. Its unusual plan, with a raised presbytery behind an arcade of carved arches, and its finely worked stone screens are unique. Together with Santa María del Naranco and San Miguel de Lillo in Oviedo, it is part of a World Heritage listing.

The church is reached by a short walk or ride up a narrow lane from the old Lena valley road near Pola de Lena. Opening hours vary and there is usually a small entry charge, so check ahead. Even if it is closed, the setting is worth it: green slopes, chestnut trees, the sound of cowbells and the motorway in the valley below.

The riding here is pure Asturias. The old N-630 climbs south past the church to the Puerto de Pajares, at about 1,380 metres the historic pass between Asturias and León, with steep gradients, tight hairpins and spectacular views when the fog lifts. The motorway, AP-66, uses the Huerna valley instead, with a toll, so the old road is quiet. Nearby, the Puerto de la Cubilla is a narrow, steep climb on a smaller road. Asturian weather is changeable, and mist and drizzle are common; roads stay damp under the trees.

The Lena valley was mining country, part of the coal basin that runs through Mieres and Langreo, and the miners' strikes of 1934 were a major event in Spanish history. Today the valley is greener and quieter. The pilgrimage route of the Camino de San Salvador passes nearby, linking León with Oviedo, and you may meet walkers on the lane.

Pola de Lena, four kilometres away, is a town of nearly thirteen thousand people with fuel, cafés and cider houses where waiters pour cider from above their heads into the glass. Fabada asturiana, a rich bean stew with chorizo and black pudding, is the dish to eat before tackling Pajares.
t.eglise san salvador@43.5,-5.4:
Tucked into a narrow valley a few kilometres south of Villaviciosa, the little church of San Salvador de Valdediós is one of the jewels of Asturian pre-Romanesque architecture. Locals call it El Conventín, the little convent, and it was consecrated at the end of the ninth century under King Alfonso III, during the period when the small Kingdom of Asturias was the only Christian state in Iberia not under Muslim rule. Its tall, narrow nave, round arches and delicate stone lattice windows give it a strangely intimate atmosphere.

Next to it stands the much larger Cistercian monastery of Santa María de Valdediós, built several centuries later, with a Romanesque church and a cloister. Together they make a peaceful ensemble, surrounded by meadows and woods, with the sound of the stream and birdsong. The valley's name means valley of God, and it feels like it.

Riding in Asturias is a joy. The roads around Villaviciosa wind through green hills, apple orchards and small villages, with good surfaces and moderate traffic. The coast road east and west offers views of cliffs, beaches and fishing villages, while the roads inland climb towards the mountains of the Cordillera Cantábrica. The weather is mild but often wet, and fog can roll in from the sea. Summer is the best time, though autumn brings beautiful colours and fewer tourists.

Villaviciosa is the capital of Asturian cider, and the hills around it are covered with apple orchards. Asturian cider is poured from a height to aerate it, a skill called escanciar, and the sidrerías of the region are lively places where cider flows freely. The Ría de Villaviciosa, an estuary nearby, is a nature reserve with salt marshes and birdlife. It was here, according to tradition, that the young future emperor Charles V first landed in Spain in 1517, having been blown off course.

Villaviciosa, about six kilometres away, has fuel, restaurants and accommodation. Colunga, to the east, is home to the Jurassic Museum of Asturias, celebrating the dinosaur footprints found along this coast. Try fabada asturiana, a rich bean stew with chorizo and morcilla, and finish with arroz con leche, rice pudding with a caramelized sugar crust.
t.alto douro wine region@41.1,-7.8:
The Douro river has been carving a gorge through the north of Portugal for millions of years, and for about two thousand years people have been planting vines on its slopes. The terraces, held up by stone walls, climb steeply from the water and rise through schist and slate in rows, and the effect, in the right season, is of a vast green staircase. The Alto Douro was the first wine region in the world to be officially demarcated, by the Marquis of Pombal in 1756, and UNESCO listed it in 2001. Port wine, the sweet fortified red that made the region famous, is still made here.

Lamego, the town on our list, is a small cathedral city on a hill above the valley, best known for its sanctuary of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, reached by a monumental staircase of baroque zigzags with hundreds of steps. It is also known for a sparkling wine, raposeira, and for smoked ham, and its pastry shops are generous. The old centre is quiet and a little faded, with granite houses, and it makes a good base for the valley, which is a short ride away.

The riding is wonderful. The N222 between Peso da Régua and Pinhão runs along the river and is often described as one of the best driving roads in the world, which is a fair summary, with a fluid sequence of bends, plenty of views over the terraced slopes, and decent asphalt. Other roads climb through the vineyards from the river to the plateau, with hairpins and narrow sections. Traffic can be slow in the harvest season, in September and October, when tractors and workers fill the lanes, but that is also when the colours are at their best, with leaves turning yellow and red. Summers are very hot, with temperatures over forty degrees in the valley.

Lamego has fuel, banks and cafes, and Peso da Régua, a short run to the north, has more. Pinhão railway station is decorated with blue-and-white tile panels showing scenes of the wine harvest, and it is a pleasant stop. If you taste at a quinta, a rider needs to be disciplined, because the wines are strong and the roads narrow and steep. The wineries often have rooms, so staying over is a good solution.
t.san miguel de lillo@43.4,-5.9:
The hill of Naranco rises just north of Oviedo, the capital of Asturias, and on its slope, among oaks and chestnuts, stand two small stone buildings that are among the oldest and strangest churches in Europe. San Miguel de Lillo is the smaller and the more battered, and it lies a few minutes above Santa María del Naranco, three kilometres from the middle of the city, in a green landscape of meadows and apple orchards.

Both were built in the mid-ninth century for King Ramiro I, who ruled the little Christian kingdom of Asturias while most of Spain was under Muslim rule. Asturian builders developed their own style in these years, a pre-Romanesque art with barrel vaults, tall slim proportions and carved decoration of an unusual freshness. At San Miguel, only part of the church survives, because the western end collapsed centuries ago, but what remains is full of surprises. The stone lattice windows are each cut from a single slab, the doorway jambs carry sculpted scenes of circus performers and a Byzantine-looking emperor, and the vaults are supported on slender, ribbed arches. UNESCO inscribed both churches in 1985. Opening hours are limited and the entrance for small groups is controlled, so check ahead.

The way up from Oviedo is a short, steep climb on a winding road through the suburbs and then the woods. The surface is fine but narrow, with blind corners, and the car park is small, so arrive early or late in the day to avoid the coach tours. The hill gives a fine view across the city to the Cantabrian mountains, which are often capped with cloud and, in winter and spring, snow. Asturias is one of the wettest parts of Spain and the weather changes constantly, so a light waterproof is sensible. The best days are in late spring and early autumn, when the light is clear and the grass is green.

Oviedo is a lively and handsome city of over two hundred thousand people, with a cathedral, a university and a statue on almost every corner. Fuel and food are easy to find, and the old town is a short ride away. Order fabada, the bean and sausage stew, and sidra, the local cider, poured from a great height into a wide glass to give it a sparkle, though locals will be amused if you try it yourself. Cheese from the nearby valleys, especially the blue Cabrales, is very strong.
t.tower of hercules@43.4,-8.4:
On a rocky headland at the edge of A Coruña, a city of about two hundred and fifty thousand people on the north-west corner of Spain, stands a grey stone tower nearly fifty-five metres tall. It is the Tower of Hercules, and it is the oldest Roman lighthouse in the world still in use, which makes it a good deal older than almost anything else that works in Europe. UNESCO inscribed it in 2009.

The Romans built it in the late first or early second century, probably under the emperor Trajan, and an inscription at the foot names the architect, Gaius Sevius Lupus, from Aeminium, now Coimbra in Portugal. It guided ships coming in from the Atlantic toward the port the Romans called Brigantium, on a coast of reefs and fog, where many ships were lost. The tower fell into disrepair in the Middle Ages, and in 1788 it was restored and clad in neoclassical masonry, which hides the Roman core, though you can see the Roman stonework through a window in the base. The name comes from a Galician legend: Hercules killed the giant Geryon here and buried his head under the tower, and the city grew around the place, with a skull and crossed bones on its coat of arms.

The landscape here is Atlantic. Waves break on the black rocks, the wind carries the smell of salt and seaweed, and the sky changes from clear blue to heavy grey within an hour. Galicia gets a great deal of rain, so waterproofs are almost always a sensible companion, and in winter the swell can be dramatic. The coast to the north and west, the Costa da Morte, the Coast of Death, is famous for shipwrecks and wild scenery, with long, empty roads and fishing villages, and it is a superb ride on a fine day.

A Coruña itself is easy to enjoy. The old town and the harbour front, with its glass-fronted galleries, lie on a narrow isthmus, and you can walk to the tower along the seafront promenade in about an hour. For a rider the city has fuel, parking and a range of cafes, and the toll motorway to Santiago de Compostela, about seventy kilometres south, makes it an easy day trip. Eat octopus, in the Galician style with paprika and olive oil, or a tortilla, and drink the white wine of Rías Baixas.
t.cathedrale de mondonedo@43.4,-7.4:
Mondoñedo is a small cathedral city in the north of Galicia, tucked into a green valley of the Masma river between the Cantabrian coast and the hills of the interior. With barely five thousand people it is one of the smallest places in Spain to have a cathedral, and the building is the reason the town exists. It was begun in the late twelfth century and finished over several centuries, with a Romanesque core, Gothic vaults and a Baroque west front with two towers. Inside, there are medieval wall paintings in the cloister and a fine stone choir, and the whole is built from the grey local granite, which turns green with lichen and gold in the evening sun.

The town has the feel of a place that has been left alone. Narrow streets climb from the river, lined with old houses with glazed balconies, and the Camino del Norte pilgrim route passes close by. It was the home of the writer Álvaro Cunqueiro, whose novels mixed Galician folklore with gentle humour, and a statue honours him in town. In the mist that often fills the valley, his world of ghosts, wolves and wandering cooks seems easy to believe in.

The riding in northern Galicia is lush and pleasant. Roads wind over green hills through eucalyptus and pine, with farms and small fields, and sudden views of the valley. Corners are medium in speed and frequent, and traffic is thin outside the larger towns. Rain is common, even in summer, and the roads can be wet and slippery under the trees, so be prepared. In clear weather the colours are intense, the green of the hills against the grey of the stone.

Mondoñedo has fuel, bakeries and bars, and Abadín is a larger village a short way to the south-east. The local cooking is hearty, with stews, pork, and the famous Galician pies called empanadas, and the cheese is soft and mild. Spring and early autumn are the best times, and winter can be wet and cold. The monastery of Sobrado dos Monxes, a Cistercian foundation, is a worthwhile detour for the same ride.
t.la foncalada@43.4,-5.8:
Oviedo has a tiny fountain that is older than almost everything else in the city, and it sits in a gap between two streets a few steps from the cathedral. La Foncalada, a little stone building with a gabled front and a pool inside, was built in the ninth century in the time of King Alfonso III, and it is the only surviving civil building of the Asturian pre-Romanesque style in the capital. Water from a spring still flows through it, and a pilgrim on the Camino Primitivo, the oldest of the routes to Santiago, passes by on the way through town. It is easy to walk past without noticing, which would be a pity.

Oviedo itself is a handsome, easy city, with a compact old centre, the Gothic cathedral with its single tower, and a lively street life built around cider. The Asturians pour their cider from a height, a practice called escanciar, to aerate it, and visitors in sidrerías are happily taught. Fabada, a stew of white beans, pork and sausage, is the traditional dish. On the hill of Naranco above the city stand two small pre-Romanesque buildings from the ninth century, Santa María del Naranco and San Miguel de Lillo, built under King Ramiro I, with delicate carving and slender arches. They look out over the valley and are among the oldest and finest buildings of their kind. Statues dot the streets, including one of Woody Allen, who made a film here.

Asturias is steep, green and wet, and the roads are great fun for a motorcyclist. Out of the city, roads climb through chestnut and eucalyptus forest to passes with views over mountains, the Picos de Europa on a clear day, and drop to fishing villages on the coast. Rain is common, and the surface can be greasy, so watch the corners. In the city, traffic is moderate and the centre is partly pedestrianised, so park outside it.

Oviedo has plenty of fuel and everything else, and Lugones and Castandiello, on the edge of town, have petrol stations too. A few hours in the old town, with a coffee and a pastry, is the right way to take the stop. Spring and early autumn give the best weather.
t.santiago de compostela@42.9,-8.5:
Whatever time you arrive in Santiago de Compostela, you will probably find someone crying in the Praza do Obradoiro. They have walked for weeks, or days, or the last hundred kilometres the pilgrim rule requires, and the cathedral at the end of it is as big and golden as they hoped. Santiago has been the goal of the Camino since the ninth century, when a hermit was said to have found the tomb of the apostle James here, and the city grew up around the shrine. The cathedral you see now is largely Romanesque in its bones, with a baroque front that glows when it is not raining, which in Galicia is a fair part of the year.

Riders come as pilgrims of a different kind, by road rather than on foot. The best arrival is from the east, through green countryside of oak woods and granite farmhouses, down roads that dip and rise like the Galician coast itself. The approach is easy and the corners generous, with surfaces that are mostly smooth, though the wet leaves of autumn can make them slippery. Once you reach the edge of the old town, park legally and leave the bike. The historic centre is largely pedestrian and the stone streets are polished to a glassy finish by rain and feet.

A few things are worth doing before you get back on the bike. Walk into the cathedral, where the giant botafumeiro, a silver incense burner, is swung on special occasions. Buy a slice of tarta de Santiago, the almond cake marked with the cross of St James. Eat pulpo a feira, octopus with paprika, or simply a bowl of caldo gallego if the weather is wet. And look up: the rooftops and gables of Santiago are worth the stiff neck.

The region label mentions the monastery of Sobrado dos Monxes, a former Cistercian abbey in the countryside to the east, and it makes a good detour if you have time, with its enormous church and cloister set amid farmland.

Santiago is a city of ninety-five thousand, so fuel, food and rooms are everywhere. Book ahead in summer and around the feast of St James on 25 July.
t.santa maria del naranco@43.4,-5.9:
There is a point on the road up Monte Naranco where Oviedo suddenly appears below you, and it is nothing like what you imagined. Spread across a valley of green hills, the capital of Asturias looks more like a country town than a city of two hundred thousand, with the cathedral tower in the middle and the sea hidden somewhere beyond the ridge. The hillside is a ride of about three kilometres from the centre, steady and winding, and it leads to one of Spain's best-loved medieval buildings.

Santa María del Naranco was built in the middle of the ninth century as part of a royal estate for King Ramiro I, and it was probably a palace hall rather than a church, only later converted to religious use. The building is a rectangle of pale stone, with an open arcaded balcony at either end, and the proportions are surprisingly graceful. Its carved decoration, with medallions and twisted ropes, is more refined than you might expect from a kingdom that was fighting for survival against the Moors. Together with the nearby church of San Miguel de Lillo, it is part of the Asturian pre-Romanesque group, listed by UNESCO in the 1980s.

The ride to the mountain from the city centre is short but pleasant, with some gentle bends and shady trees, and the view alone is worth it on a clear day. Visits to the interior are usually timed and ticketed, so check the arrangements before arriving, particularly on Mondays when some monuments close.

Come in late afternoon, if you can, when the light on the stone softens and the city turns gold below. Asturias is green because it rains, and the weather can change fast, so carry a waterproof even when the morning looks fine.

Oviedo has all the fuel, food and rooms a rider could want. This is cider country, and the traditional bars pour it from a height, so wait for a proper sidrería and order a bottle with some fabada, the big white bean stew that is the local pride.
Asturias had a king who believed in building well, and Alfonso II, known as the Chaste, is the reason the church of San Julián de los Prados exists. He made Oviedo his capital in the early ninth century, and the basilica, known locally as Santullano, was raised outside the city walls around the year 830. Inside, the walls are covered with mural decoration that imitates Roman architecture, with painted columns, curtains and buildings in perspective, all in soft red, ochre and blue. It is astonishing to see such work surviving from the ninth century, and the effect of these painted walls, especially in the long, narrow side chapels, is of a church that has been dressed for a party that never ended. UNESCO included it in the Oviedo and Kingdom of the Asturias listing in the 1980s.
