The church is a short ride from the centre, and the best approach is to park in the nearby streets rather than take the bike into the dense heart of the old town. Opening hours are limited and vary by season, so look at the current schedule before you go, and expect to pay a small fee or join a short guided visit.

Oviedo is also the beginning of the Camino Primitivo, the original pilgrimage route to Santiago, which pilgrims follow west into the Asturian mountains. Several of them will pass the church on their way. Their scallop shells and walking sticks are a common sight on these streets.

With over two hundred thousand people, Oviedo has all the fuel, food and accommodation you might need. Eat well: fabada, cheeses such as Cabrales and a bottle of cider are the local pleasures.
t.coimbra@40.2,-8.4:
Coimbra is a hill town that happens to hold one of the oldest universities in Europe. The old city climbs up from the Mondego river in a tangle of steep, cobbled lanes, with the university buildings at the summit, and in the evenings the sound of fado drifts down from taverns and small squares. The Coimbra version of fado is different from the Lisbon one, sung traditionally by men, often students in black capes, and tied to serenades beneath windows.

The university dates from 1290 and moved to its present site in 1537, in what had been a royal palace. The Joanina Library, a baroque hall of gilded shelves and painted ceilings built in the eighteenth century, is one of the most beautiful in the world, and the staff keep a colony of bats to protect the books from insects, covering the furniture at night. UNESCO inscribed the university in 2013. Coimbra was the capital of Portugal for a time in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and the legend of Ines de Castro, the lover of a prince who was murdered, and crowned queen after death, is told here.

The Estrada Nacional 2, which runs for about seven hundred kilometres from Chaves in the north to Faro in the south, passes through the region, and Coimbra is a natural place for the ride to pause. The road in this area is mostly good, with moderate traffic, and the streets in the old town are steep and slippery when wet. Parking is easiest on the river side, and a short walk takes you up to the Alta.

With over a hundred thousand people, Coimbra offers fuel, food and rooms in all price ranges. The traditional dish here is chanfana, goat cooked in red wine, and the pastries are very sweet. Nearby, Conimbriga has some of the best-preserved Roman remains in Portugal, with mosaics and a house with fountains, and is easy to reach by bike. Spring and autumn are comfortable, with warm days and cool evenings.
t.monuments of oviedo and the kingdom of t:
Oviedo is a capital that started as a monastery. In the early ninth century King Alfonso II of Asturias moved his court here, built a church dedicated to the Saviour, and began to create a little kingdom out of the mountains that had resisted the Moors, and the buildings that followed form one of the most distinctive groups of early medieval architecture in Europe. UNESCO lists the Monuments of Oviedo and the Kingdom of the Asturias, and the best of them stand on the slopes of Monte Naranco, above the city: Santa María del Naranco, a palace hall of King Ramiro I built in the 840s and later used as a church, and San Miguel de Lillo, a slender church nearby.

Santa María del Naranco is a marvel. Its proportions are harmonious, with an arcaded gallery at each end, and the stone vaults and sculpted medallions show an architecture that has no direct parallel in its time. San Miguel de Lillo survives only in part, but its carved window lattices and doorway reliefs are exquisite. In the city, the Cámara Santa of the cathedral houses the Cross of the Angels, a gold and jewel cross given by Alfonso II in 808, and the Victory Cross, associated with Pelayo and the battle of Covadonga.

The ride up Naranco from the city is short and steep, with a few hairpins and a view of Oviedo. Beyond, the roads of Asturias are a rider's delight: the climb to the Lagos de Covadonga, the mountain passes of Pajares and San Isidro, and the winding coastal roads. Asturias is green because it is wet, so carry waterproofs, and expect fog on the high ground. Fuel is plentiful in Oviedo and in Lugones, five kilometres away.

Eat here, too. Oviedo is the home of fabada, the white bean and sausage stew, of cider poured from a height into a wide glass, of the cachopo, a vast breaded veal and ham cutlet, and of sweet pastries such as the carbayón. A statue of Woody Allen on a street corner commemorates his love of the city. Park the bike in a car park and walk, since the old centre is largely pedestrian.
t.viseu@40.7,-7.9:
Viseu sits on a granite plateau in the middle of northern Portugal, and for a rider on the Estrada Nacional 2 it makes a natural halfway point between the Douro and the Tagus. It is a handsome, orderly city of about twenty-six thousand within its core, with a cathedral square, a medieval centre of granite houses, and a long reputation for good living. The city is the capital of the Dão wine region, whose reds, based on the Touriga Nacional grape, are some of the most elegant in Portugal, and the vineyards lie on the sheltered slopes around it, protected by mountains from the Atlantic rain.

The great name in Viseu is Grão Vasco, the nickname of the painter Vasco Fernandes, who worked here in the early sixteenth century and whose altarpieces fill the museum beside the cathedral. A statue of Viriato, the Lusitanian chieftain who held out against the Romans, stands outside the town, and the Viseu district claims him as its own. In August and September, the ancient fair of São Mateus, which has been held since the late fourteenth century, fills the city with stalls, music and fairground rides, and is one of the oldest and biggest fairs in the country.

The N2, Portugal's answer to Route 66, runs the whole length of the country from Chaves in the north to Faro in the south, and Viseu lies close to its path. The riding through the Dão country is fine, with sweeping bends through pine forest, vineyards and granite villages, and views of the Serra da Estrela and the Caramulo mountains. Surface quality varies, from smooth new tarmac to old patched sections, and in towns the cobbles can be slippery when wet. Traffic is moderate, and in autumn the harvest brings tractors and trailers onto the road.

Fuel, food and coffee are all easy in the city, which has several supermarkets and many restaurants. The regional food is hearty and delicious, with roast kid, veal from the Lafões area, and cheese from the nearby Serra da Estrela, which is soft, creamy and best eaten with a spoon. Rojões, chunks of pork stewed in wine, are another local classic, and of course the Dão wine goes well with all of them.

Linger a while in the old town, with its narrow streets and cafés, and sit in the square by the cathedral with an espresso and a custard tart. The light in the late afternoon on the granite is warm and golden, and the pace of life is gentle.
t.zamora@41.5,-5.7:
Zamora is a city built on a rock above the Duero, and it is overlooked in a way that suits its quiet temperament. The old town sits on a ridge on the north bank, with a medieval stone bridge reaching across the river, and the whole place feels slightly apart from the rest of the busy plain around it. It is said to have more Romanesque churches than any other city in Europe, about two dozen, built mostly in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries when Zamora was a frontier town between the Christian north and the Moorish south. Their rounded arches and plain stone walls give the streets a sober, weathered look that is especially fine in evening light.

The cathedral, small by the standards of Spain, has an unusual dome covered in scale-like stone tiles that looks almost Byzantine, and it is a good landmark when you are looking for the centre. The city is also known for its Holy Week processions, which are some of the most solemn in the country, with hooded brotherhoods marching in silence through the old streets. If you pass through in the days before Easter, you will find the roads blocked and the hotels full.

The Ruta de la Plata follows an ancient line that the Romans used to carry silver and other goods from the mines of the south to the north, and later pilgrims used it too, on their way to Santiago. Today the road runs across the high, open plateau of the northern meseta, with long views, a lot of wheat and sunflowers, and few bends. It is good cruising but not twisty riding, and the wind can be strong. For the best conditions, aim for spring, when the fields are green and poppies grow beside the road, or early autumn.

With around sixty-five thousand residents, Zamora has fuel in abundance and plenty of bars. A traditional dish is arroz a la zamorana, made with pork, and the local sheep's milk cheese is excellent. A coffee in the main square or on the bank of the Duero is a gentle way to pass the middle of the day, and the shade under the old walls is welcome in summer, when the plain can be very hot.
t.leon@42.6,-5.6:
León has been a city for nearly two thousand years, since a Roman legion made camp here, and the old rectangle of the Roman walls is still partly visible in the heart of the town. The name itself comes from the legion, not from the lion that now sits on the city's flag, though locals prefer the lion. In the Middle Ages León was the capital of a kingdom, and later it became a major stop on the pilgrim road to Santiago, so the old quarter is full of churches, monasteries and inns that pilgrims used for rest.

The three things to see are the cathedral, the Basilica of San Isidoro and the Hostal de San Marcos. The cathedral is Gothic, light and slender, and its walls are almost entirely made of stained glass, so that on a sunny morning the interior glows red and blue. San Isidoro, nearby, holds a royal burial chamber with twelfth-century wall paintings that are some of the best Romanesque frescoes in Europe. The Hostal de San Marcos, a sixteenth-century former convent, is now a luxurious hotel, with an elaborately carved front facing the river. Even Gaudí left a mark, with a neo-Gothic building called the Casa Botines on the main square.

At the end of a long ride south to north across the meseta, León makes a very good finish. With over a hundred thousand people, it has plenty of fuel, bike-friendly parking on the edge of the old town and hotels for every budget. In the evening the narrow streets of the Barrio Húmedo fill with people going from bar to bar, and in the traditional way each drink comes with a free small plate of food, so it is possible to dine well without ever sitting down. The cured meats, especially the local cecina, a smoked beef, deserve a try, and so do the blood sausages.

To the north of the city the Cantabrian Mountains rise, and the roads there are among the best in northern Spain, with passes and gorges, but that is for another day. Today you roll in off the plateau, find a place to park, and walk. Spring and autumn are best, because winter nights can be bitterly cold and summer afternoons are hot.
t.malpica@43.3,-8.8:
Malpica is where the Costa da Morte, the Coast of Death, begins in earnest. The name sounds dramatic and it is earned. This long stretch of Galician coast, bristling with granite headlands, shoals and fog, has seen more shipwrecks than almost anywhere in Europe, and the people here have a long history of watching the sea for trouble and for the cargo that it sometimes delivered. Today Malpica is a working fishing port of about seven thousand people on a deep bay, with a harbour full of brightly coloured boats and a small town of white houses climbing the hill behind it.

The sea is the town's business. Out beyond the harbour lie the Sisargas islands, three granite islets that are a bird sanctuary and a place of old legends. They can be visited by boat in summer, and they hold huge colonies of gulls, shags and cormorants. The rocks along this shore are also famed for percebes, goose barnacles, a delicacy that is harvested by hand from the waves at great personal risk. Percebes are pricey and look unappealing, rather like dinosaur toes, but they taste of the cold sea, and Malpica is one of the best places to try them. Octopus, fried fish and mussels are also on every menu.

For a rider, Malpica is a good first stop on a long coastal day. The roads leading to the town from Carballo cross rolling country of pine, eucalyptus and small farms, with dry-stone walls and granite crosses at the junctions. The surface is usually fine, if narrow in places, and the corners are gentle. Along the coast, the road climbs and dips between fishing villages and headlands, with views of long beaches and big Atlantic swells. Fog can come in quickly, and the wind off the sea is strong and cool. In the dry season, you can ride with long, sunny views, but in wet weather the granite surfaces and wet leaves require extra care.

Malpica has fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat, so it is a fine place to resupply before heading west and south along the coast. The more remote stretches toward Laxe have fewer services. Carballo, about fifteen kilometres inland, is a bigger town with everything.

Climb the hill to the Monte Atalaia viewpoint, where the whole bay lies spread out below you, and watch the fishing boats come home.
t.laxe@43.2,-9.0:
Laxe is easy to like because it does not try very hard. A fishing town of a few thousand people tucked into a curved bay on the Costa da Morte, it has a harbour where boats unload the day's catch, a long sandy beach that curves round the bay, and a low white skyline of houses. In summer, Galician families spread out on the sand, and in winter the Atlantic throws huge swells against the headland, so that the town feels like the last outpost before the open sea.

The coast around Laxe is the heart of the Costa da Morte, a name that refers to its long record of shipwrecks. Granite reefs, thick fog and powerful currents have made this one of the most dangerous stretches of coast in Europe, and local folklore is full of stories of lost ships and wreckers. The lighthouses along the coast, built in the nineteenth century, were a response to this, and they still stand on the headlands. Inland a short distance, the Dolmen of Dombate, a megalithic burial chamber several thousand years old, survives under a protective roof in a field, and is a reminder that people have lived and buried their dead here since long before the Romans arrived.

The riding along the coast is excellent. The roads link small fishing villages and headlands through a landscape of pines, gorse and granite outcrops, with big sea views opening and closing. Corners are fairly gentle but regular, and the surface varies from smooth to patched, particularly where the sea air has done its work. Traffic is light outside August, and the pace of life is slow. From Laxe, the coast road runs west toward Camariñas and the cape, through some of the most beautiful and empty stretches of Galicia, with long beaches and wind-bent trees.

Laxe has shops, a few cafés and bars, and a fuel station should be available in town, but in this sparsely populated area it is wise to fill up whenever you see a pump. Camariñas, about seventeen kilometres away, is the larger option. The bars by the harbour serve fresh seafood, octopus Galician style with paprika and olive oil, and cold white wine.

Walk to the end of the breakwater at dusk to watch the boats come in, and see how the light turns the bay silver.
t.cape vilan@43.2,-9.2:
Cabo Vilán is a headland of dark rock, flogged by wind and swell, with a lighthouse at the end that has a place in the history of Spain. When its lamp was first lit in 1896, it was the first electrically powered lighthouse in the country, a statement of faith in the new technology on a coast that had long been the graveyard of ships. The tower is a plain, stout shape, with a small museum inside on the history of shipwrecks and lights, and the view from the foot takes in the roaring Atlantic and the long line of the Costa da Morte.

The shipwrecks are the reason for all of it. In 1890, the British Royal Navy training ship HMS Serpent was driven onto the rocks near here in a storm, and about 170 sailors drowned, with only three survivors. The dead were buried in a small walled cemetery on the coast near Camariñas, known as the English Cemetery, which stands in a quiet spot above the sea and is a moving place to stop. The locals helped with the rescue and the burial, and the story has become part of the local memory. The wild nature of the shore explains why so many ships have been lost.

Camariñas, a few kilometres to the east, is better known for its lace. For generations the women of the town made bobbin lace, a technique that involves dozens of wooden bobbins and a pillow, and the tradition continues in workshops and in the annual festival. The lace-makers' work is shown at a local museum and on the streets in summer, where women sit at doorsteps working on delicate patterns. It is a gentle contrast with the violence of the coast.

The road to the cape runs along the ria, a deep inlet, from Camariñas, then climbs over a bare headland of heather and granite. The surface is good, and the corners are open, but the wind can be fierce and gusts may catch you by surprise on exposed bends. Fog is common, and when it rolls in the lighthouse horn sounds. Keep your speed modest and your visor clean. The approach is short, so even a half-hour detour from the main road is worth it.

Camariñas, about four kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and several seafood restaurants. Mugía, six kilometres on, is the next major stop on the coast. Try the local octopus, grilled sea bream or a bowl of caldo gallego, a thick soup of beans, greens and pork that warms you after the wind. Storm days are dramatic, with waves exploding on the rocks, but check conditions and stay well back.
t.muxia@43.1,-9.2:
Muxía clings to the end of a rocky peninsula, and its church sits on the very edge of the sea. The Santuario da Virxe da Barca stands on a ledge of granite where the waves break on three sides, and according to the legend, the Virgin Mary appeared here in a stone boat to encourage Saint James when he was preaching in Galicia. The great stones beside the church, including one that is said to rock when you stand on it, are the remains of that boat's sail, rudder and hull. The local pilgrims believe passing under or touching them can cure ailments.

The sanctuary has been a place of pilgrimage for centuries, and today it is an end point for many walkers on the Camino de Santiago, who continue on foot to the coast after reaching Santiago. In December 2013, the church was struck by lightning and burned, a loss that shocked the community, and it has since been restored. Nearby stands a monument to the oil tanker Prestige, which sank off this coast in 2002 and covered the shore in thick black oil. Muxía was one of the worst-hit towns, and thousands of volunteers came from across Spain to clean the beaches by hand. The monument, a tall split stone known as A Ferida, the Wound, commemorates both the disaster and the volunteer effort.

The town itself is a small fishing port of about five thousand people with a harbour full of boats, a few streets of white houses and a mood of salt and wind. The riding from Camariñas along the coast is a pleasure, with a road that winds between gorse-covered hills and the sea, with open views of granite and surf. The surface is generally good, the bends are moderate, and the wind and fog require respect. In summer the roads fill with pilgrims, cyclists and holidaymakers, so avoid the middle of the day.

Muxía has fuel, a few supermarkets and bars, and several restaurants that serve octopus, fish and shellfish. Camariñas is just over four kilometres to the south, and Fisterra, the so-called end of the world, lies farther down the coast. The two together make a good day.

Sit on the rocks by the sanctuary and listen to the sea, which has the dull boom of something that has been doing this for a very long time.
t.covadonga@43.3,-5.1:
Ask a Spaniard where their country's story starts again after the Moorish conquest and many will say here, in a green fold of the Picos de Europa, a few kilometres up the valley from Cangas de Onís. The tradition says a Visigothic noble named Pelayo and a small band of Asturians beat a Muslim force in the hills around 722, and the kingdom of Asturias grew from it. Whether the battle was as grand as the legend or a skirmish blown up later, historians still argue, but the place carries the weight regardless. Pelayo is buried in the cave.

That cave, the Santa Cueva, holds a shrine to the Virgin, the Santina, set under a rock overhang with a waterfall spilling beside it into a pool. Above stands the twin-spired pink basilica, a nineteenth-century building, and on the terrace you will meet pilgrims, school groups and bikers all taking the same photographs. It is busy, and it is meant to be. Park, walk the short paths, and let the scale of the limestone walls settle in.

The road here is the AS-262 and its siblings, climbing out of Cangas de Onís along the Güeña river through meadows, chestnuts and beech, with stone hórreos on stilts in the village yards. It is a gentle, pretty approach, not a technical one, and the surface is decent. The real weather lesson of the Picos comes with the altitude. The Atlantic is only a short distance north, so cloud piles up against the peaks, and a bright morning can turn to drizzle by noon. Summer weekends and Easter are the crowded times, and when the road above is busy, access to the lakes can be controlled, so check before you commit your day to it.

Cangas de Onís has fuel, cafés and the Roman-style bridge with the hanging cross, which is worth a look. Asturias runs on cider poured from a height, bean-and-sausage stew called fabada, and strong blue cheeses, and any bar around here will serve you all three without ceremony. If you are staying on the bike, stick to the coffee and a slice of cheese and save the cider for the evening.
t.torre@40.3,-7.6:
The highest point of mainland Portugal is a disappointment for about thirty seconds and then a joy. Torre is a bare, rounded granite summit in the Serra da Estrela at 1,993 metres, and it is seven metres short of two thousand. Some years ago a stone tower was built on top to make up the difference, so the monument can claim the round number even if the mountain cannot. Around it the plateau is a landscape of boulders, thin grass, small lakes and wind, and in clear weather the view is vast, running across the plains of the Beira to the Spanish border.

This high country was shaped by glaciers in the last ice age, which scoured the broad valley of the Zêzere River and left behind rounded rocks and glacial lakes. The mountains are cold and often cloudy, with snow from late autumn to spring, and it is the only place in Portugal where people ski in any numbers. In summer sheep graze the slopes, and shepherds still make Serra da Estrela cheese, a soft, creamy sheep's milk cheese that you can buy in the shops of Covilhã and Manteigas. The breed of mountain dog named for the range, big and thick-coated, was bred to guard these flocks.

The road up from Covilhã is a proper mountain climb, with long bends, big views and a high, open feel as you leave the trees. The tarmac is generally good, but weather rules everything: fog can reduce visibility to a few metres, wind makes the exposed plateau cold even in summer, and in winter the road may be closed by snow or ice. Choose a clear day, go early, and bring warm layers and waterproofs. Mid-summer weekends can bring heavy traffic, so weekdays are quieter.

There are small shops and snack stalls near the summit selling cheese, sausages, honey and warm clothes, which are useful when the wind bites. The nearest larger town is Covilhã, about ten kilometres away, where you will find petrol stations, restaurants and everything else, and Manteigas, a smaller town in the glacial valley, makes a pleasant lunch stop with a spa tradition. Fill the tank before you climb, because nothing at the top will help you.

When the mist lifts and the plateau opens, it feels like another country altogether, closer to the Scottish hills than to the Mediterranean south.
t.pinhao@41.2,-7.5:
Pinhão is a small town on the Douro whose most memorable building is a railway station. Inside, the walls are covered in blue-and-white azulejo tiles that show scenes of wine harvests and life along the river, painted in the early twentieth century, and they give the little platform the look of a gallery. The trains no longer carry port wine barrels downriver, but a line still runs through the valley, and a few tourist trains stop here.

The setting is the real show. The Douro flows through a narrow valley in northern Portugal, and its slopes are terraced from river to ridge with vineyards that have been cultivated for centuries, a landscape listed as a World Heritage cultural landscape. Port wine was born here, and the quintas, or wine estates, scattered along the river are still the lifeblood of the region. The schist hillsides retain heat, the vines grow in thin stony soil, and the smell of fermenting grapes drifts through the valley in September.

The N222, which runs along the river from Peso da Régua to Pinhão and beyond, has been voted one of the best driving roads in the world, and it deserves it. It is not wild or fast, but it is beautifully made, with smooth tarmac, an endless run of easy bends, the river glittering beside you and terraces rising on both sides. Traffic is generally light, though tourist coaches appear in high season, and in the autumn harvest tractors and grape trucks mean you should slow down. The best times are spring, when the vines are fresh green, and autumn, when they turn red and gold; in July and August it is very hot, with the schist radiating heat.

In Pinhão, the riverfront has cafés and restaurants, and you can take a boat trip or taste wine at quintas nearby, though if you are riding you should be sensible about how much you sample. Simple Portuguese food, grilled meat, bacalhau and sweet pastries, pairs well with a coffee by the water. Fuel is not always available in the town itself, so the larger places nearby such as Régua or Tabuaço are safer, and it is a good idea to fill up before heading into the valley.

Wander down to the river, take in the quiet pace of the village, and watch the barges and boats drift by.
t.peso da regua river@41.2,-7.8:
Régua sits where the Douro valley opens enough to hold a town, and it has been the commercial heart of the wine country for a very long time. In 1756 the Portuguese crown drew a boundary around the vineyards of the upper Douro, making it one of the first officially demarcated wine regions in the world, and the town's role as a market and shipping point goes back further. Port wine from the high terraces was loaded onto flat-bottomed rabelo boats here and floated down to the lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia, near Porto, a journey that took days and cost many a boatman his life in the rapids.

The river view is the reason for the stop. From the quay and the riverside gardens you look across a broad green stretch of water to slopes combed into terraces, the stone walls built from the local schist and the vines growing in thin, stony soil that seems to have no business supporting anything. The geometry is extraordinary, with each terrace following the contour of the hill, and the colours shift with the season, green in summer, gold and red in October when the harvest ends. A railway line runs along the bank, and slow trains still rattle past, a pleasure to watch from the water's edge.

The ride along the river is among the best in Portugal. The N222 between Régua and Pinhão is often named one of the finest driving roads in the world, and it has the surface and the curves to deserve it, with long, flowing bends beside the river and views of the terraces on the opposite bank. Traffic is light outside the harvest and summer weekend peaks, though trucks and tractors appear in the vintage season. In high summer the heat in the valley is fierce, and a ride in the early morning or late afternoon is far more pleasant.

Régua is a town of about five thousand people at its centre, with a larger municipality around it, and it has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés. Lamego, a few kilometres away, is bigger and well known for its baroque sanctuary at the top of a long monumental staircase. The Douro Museum in Régua tells the story of the region and its wine.

Sit on the riverfront with a coffee and a pastel de nata, and watch the light change. If you have the time, a short river cruise lets you see the terraces from the water, as the boatmen once did.
t.pinhao vineyards@41.2,-7.5:
Pinhão is a small town in the heart of the Douro wine country, and arriving by the river road feels like entering the engine room of Port. The little town sits where the Pinhão river meets the Douro, with terraced vineyards rising on all sides, and many of the great estates, called quintas, lie within a few kilometres. The scale of the landscape is hard to take in at first. Every slope is cut into terraces, held by dry stone walls that took generations to build, and the schist soil is so poor that the vines have to send their roots deep to find water.

The railway station is a small treasure. Its walls are covered in blue and white tiles, called azulejos, painted in the early twentieth century, showing scenes of the grape harvest and views of the valley. It is a quiet and charming bit of folk art, and worth stepping off the road to see. The harvest itself, the vindima, takes place from September to October, and in some quintas grapes are still crushed by foot in stone troughs, a tradition that survives partly for the pleasure of it. If you arrive in this season, the valley smells of fermenting fruit and the roads are busy with tractors.

The riding here is rewarding but needs care. The N222 and its neighbouring roads follow the river, with sweeping views and open bends, and many corners are cambered or edged with loose gravel from the vineyards. Heat shimmer rises in summer, and the surface can be slippery with grape juice or mud in the picking season. Tractors and lorries are common, and they take up the whole lane, so leave room and patience. Evening light on the terraces is spectacular, turning the schist the colour of honey.

Food is simple and good. Local menus feature grilled meats, roast kid or lamb, bacalhau in various forms, and regional cheeses, along with bread and olive oil that taste of the place. Many restaurants and wine estates offer lunch with views, and the wines, both red table wines and Port, are poured generously. If you are riding, treat a tasting as a tasting and not a meal.

Fuel is not in Pinhão in large amounts, and Vilela and Tabuaço, a few kilometres away, are the nearest bigger places with services. Fill up in Régua before you go further upriver.
t.quinta do fariseu@41.1,-7.1:
Quinta do Fariseu is a farm in the Coa valley in northern Portugal that sits on one of the great stories of European archaeology. In the 1990s, engineers preparing a dam on the Coa River came upon thousands of engravings carved on the schist rock faces along the valley, figures of horses, aurochs, ibex and deer, scratched into the stone by hunters thousands of years ago. Many date to the Upper Palaeolithic, some twenty thousand years old or more, which makes them as old as the paintings in the great caves of France and Spain. The find caused a public campaign, and the dam was cancelled, a rare triumph of heritage over engineering. Today the Coa Valley is a UNESCO site, together with its Spanish counterpart at Siega Verde.

The engravings are lightly incised and tricky to see, and the best viewing is in raking light, in the early morning or late afternoon, when the shadows make the lines show. Visits are by guided tour only, usually in four-wheel-drive vehicles and often with advance booking, and the guides can point out figures that you would otherwise miss. The tours run all year, though they can be cancelled in extreme heat, and it is sensible to book ahead in high season.

The countryside is a classic of the Douro region, with steep, dry hills, terraced vineyards, almond and olive groves, and old stone villages. The landscape is hot and dry in summer and cold in winter, with a remarkable spring when the almond trees bloom, normally in February. The Douro Valley, a short drive south, is a UNESCO wine region, and port wine comes from here.

For riding, the roads in this part of Portugal are good, with plenty of curves and little traffic. National roads wind across plateaus and drop into river gorges, and some of them are among the best motorcycle roads in the country. Surfaces can be rough in places, with patches of gravel, and in summer the heat is intense. Vila Nova de Foz Coa, 3.5 kilometres away, has fuel stations, restaurants and a good museum, the Coa Museum, which sits above the river and explains the finds. Torre de Moncorvo, a little further, is known for its almonds and iron ore. Local food is robust, with roast kid, cured sausages and the good wine of the region.
t.ribeirinha@41.0,-7.1:
Ribeirinha is a quiet corner of the Coa valley, and the interest of the place is the whole valley rather than one spot. Along some seventeen kilometres of the Coa River, the schist cliffs carry thousands of engravings from the Upper Palaeolithic, drawn by people who hunted across this landscape twenty thousand years ago and more. Three main sites are open to visitors, Penascosa, Canada do Inferno and Ribeira de Piscos, and each has a different character, set in different bends of the river. The valley is a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the open-air engravings at Siega Verde in Spain, which lie over the border in the province of Salamanca.

The landscape is the Portuguese interior at its most appealing, a high, hot, thinly peopled country of granite and schist, holm oak, cork and broom. The valley itself is cut deep into the plateau, with steep slopes of rock and scrub dropping to the river, and in spring the hillsides turn gold with broom and white with cistus. Griffon vultures and Bonelli's eagles circle on the thermals. The river, the Coa, runs north to meet the Douro and is a quiet, clear stream in summer.

The riding around Ribeirinha is the point. Country roads connect small villages of grey stone, and the curves are sharp and frequent, with fast, open stretches across the plateau. Traffic is sparse, so you may ride for half an hour without meeting a car. The surface is variable, with smooth asphalt and patched sections, and the occasional goat or tractor appears around a corner. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Summer temperatures often exceed forty degrees, and winter nights are cold, with frost on the high ground.

Vila Nova de Foz Coa is the nearest large town, about twelve kilometres away, with fuel, a supermarket and restaurants. Meda, to the south, is smaller, with basic services. Almond and olive oil are local products, and the area has a reputation for good bread and roast meat. If you want to visit the engravings, book a guided tour at the Coa Museum in Foz Coa, where the guides take small groups to the sites.

Not far to the west, the Douro road known as the N222 is often called the best driving road in the world, a claim made by a car magazine and repeated by every rider who has taken it. t.gijon@43.5,-5.7:
Gijón stands on a rocky headland on the Bay of Biscay, in the heart of Asturias, and the Ruta de la Plata, which began far to the south in the hot plains of Extremadura, ends here with a gust of Atlantic air. The route follows an old road whose name comes from the Arabic word for a paved way, and which carried Roman legions, medieval pilgrims and merchants between the south and the north of Spain. After the dry high country of the meseta, arriving at the cold, green coast is like entering another country, and in a sense it is.

The old quarter of Gijón, Cimavilla, sits on the headland, a warren of narrow streets and fishermen's houses, with a small harbour below and the hill of Santa Catalina above. On the hilltop stands a huge abstract sculpture by the Basque artist Eduardo Chillida, called Elogio del Horizonte, Praise of the Horizon, a curved concrete structure that frames the sea and the sky and booms in the wind. Nearby, beneath the old town, you can visit the remains of a Roman bathhouse.

Asturias is cider country, and Gijón is its capital. The drink is poured from a great height, held high above the head, into a glass held low, a showy technique that aerates the cider and is performed in countless bars. Order a bottle with a plate of fabada, the local bean stew, or grilled sardines, and the locals will teach you how to do it. The weather is mild but wet, and the Asturians have a word for the fine, constant drizzle that drifts in from the sea, called orbayu.

Gijón is a city of nearly 280,000, with plenty of fuel, restaurants and parking, and it makes a fine place to finish a ride and rest. Park near the beach of San Lorenzo, a long curve of sand beneath a promenade, and walk along it at the end of the day. The sound of the surf and the smell of salt and wet stone are a good reward for a long journey.
t.cape finisterre@42.9,-9.3:
The Romans thought the world ended here, which is why they called it Finis Terrae. It is not actually the westernmost point of Spain, a title that belongs to a cape a bit farther up the coast, but nobody visiting at sunset is inclined to argue. The headland of Cape Finisterre, Cabo Fisterra in Galician, pokes out into the Atlantic with a lighthouse on its tip, a stone marker for kilometre zero and a view over a sea that goes on to the horizon. For centuries, pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago have continued on foot to this point, and by tradition some burn their boots or clothes on the rocks to mark the end of the walk.

The coast around is called the Costa da Morte, the Coast of Death, because of the many ships that were wrecked here on the rocks and shoals in storms and fog. The sea can be spectacular and cruel, with big swells breaking against the granite, and in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries a number of famous wrecks occurred, among them HMS Serpent in 1890, whose British sailors are buried in a cemetery near Camariñas. The Prestige oil spill of 2002 also hit this coast hard, and the people of Galicia turned out in force to clean it up.

For motorcyclists, the road to the cape is a pleasure. It winds through villages of grey granite houses, past small harbours and eucalyptus woods, with the sea appearing and disappearing, and the curves are gentle but constant. The tarmac is mostly good, though wet leaves and fog can make it slippery, and the wind on the headland is strong enough to push a bike sideways. The lighthouse, built in the nineteenth century, stands on the point, and there is a small car park with a few stalls selling souvenirs and a bar where you can have a coffee or a bocadillo.

Fisterra, the nearest town, has about five thousand people and a small harbour, with fuel, shops and restaurants serving fresh seafood. Try the percebes, the barnacles that are gathered from the surf rocks, if you are feeling bold, and a glass of Albariño. The fishing port at Corcubión and the larger town of Cee lie a few kilometres further along the coast. Come at sunset if you can, bring a jacket, and stay until the light is gone. The air smells of salt, gorse and woodsmoke.
t.gouveia@40.5,-7.6:
Gouveia is where the Serra da Estrela stops being a map feature and turns into somewhere people live. It is an old granite town on the western flank of the mountains, with solid stone houses, a mid-sized main square and a long history of sheep, wool and cheese. At the end of a day crossing Portugal's highest mainland range, it makes a good place to get off the bike, because the climate here is gentler than up on the plateau and the evenings are mild.

The mountains behind it are the interesting part. The Serra da Estrela is the highest range in mainland Portugal, with the summit at the Torre close to two thousand metres, and its character is almost un-Iberian: round granite domes, boulder fields, small lakes, heather and broom, and valleys scraped into a clean U shape by glaciers during the ice ages. The Zêzere river runs in one of those valleys on the eastern side, near Manteigas, and the contrast with the dry plains beyond is striking. Snow lies here in winter, and in late autumn and spring fog can drop on the upper road with almost no warning, so look at the sky before committing.

Ride-wise, you arrive from the high road in a long descent of smooth bends, with wide views and not much traffic outside holiday weekends. The surface is generally good and the curves are open, so you can ride it with a bit of rhythm, though livestock and the occasional dog on the road deserve respect. Late spring, when the broom flowers yellow across the slopes, and early autumn are the best times; August is hot below and busy above.

The great local product is Serra da Estrela cheese, made from sheep's milk and curdled with thistle flower, soft enough to eat with a spoon when it is properly ripe. Ask for it with bread and a bit of local wine. The sheepdog of the region, the cão da Serra da Estrela, is a big, calm, slightly serious animal, and you may meet one. Fuel is simplest in Seia, about thirteen kilometres away, which is a bigger town with several stations and plenty of cafes, and Gouveia itself has the usual small-town options.

Porto stacks itself up the north bank of the Douro like a deck of cards, with the tiled houses and church towers tumbling down toward the river and the iron arch of the Dom Luís bridge holding it all together. The city has about a quarter of a million people, a lot of granite, and a love of tripe and francesinha, a sandwich of steak, sausage and ham covered with melted cheese and a beer-and-tomato sauce. The Ribeira district along the water is a World Heritage site and a good place to wander, if you do not mind the steep, polished cobbles and the crowds.

Port wine is the reason for the name and the money. It is made in the Douro Valley upriver and aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the water from Porto, where the barrels sit in cool warehouses and the big names have their signs on the roofs. The British had a large hand in its history, and some of the families still carry English surnames. A tasting in a lodge is easy to arrange, though perhaps best saved for the end of a riding day.

The Douro valley itself is the draw for riders. The N222 follows the river upstream through terraced vineyards that climb the steep schist slopes in neat lines, with the road hugging the bank or climbing in short bends to give views over the water. It has been named in magazines as one of the best driving roads in the world, and traffic is light outside harvest and peak summer. Autumn brings red and gold to the vines, and spring brings green. Summer afternoons are fiercely hot in the valley.

From Porto, the first part of any ride is urban, with tram lines, wet cobbles and tight junctions that need care, especially after rain. The motorway east along the Douro is quick, and many riders use it to reach the valley before returning on slower roads. Bom Jesus do Monte, to the north near Braga, is a pilgrimage church at the top of a grand baroque staircase, worth the detour for the view.

Fuel is no problem in a big city, and stations line the ring road. Most Portuguese motorways are tolled, some with electronic gates, so it helps to know your system. Be careful on the slick stone of the old town, and leave the bike in a secure car park rather than on the street.
